18. The above are all the oral evidence to prove the prosecution case. From the evidence discussed, it is clear that the Police Officer PWs. 3 and 9 recovered PW 5 Rina along with appellant Nos. 1-4 from a boat in the river Piara on 2-5-84 at about 3-30 PM while the boat was proceeding towards Subidkhali at a distance from Patuakhali town. This fact is not disputed or challenged by the defence. The only point for determination is whether Rina voluntarily went with the accused appellants on her way to school on the date of occurrence as alleged by the defence, or whether she was forcibly taken away from near the residence of Kazi Sb. while she was going to school along with the school Ayah Feroja and some other girl students. Both Rina PW 5 and her father PW 1 said that Rina was taken forcibly by the accused persons but no other witness is examined to prove this forcible abduction of kidnapping as alleged by the prosecution. It may be pointed out that the school Ayah Feroja Begum with whom PW 5 Rina was admittedly going to school, was not examined to prove the prosecution case, although, she was cited as witness No. 4 in the charge-sheet. No explanation was offered for her non examination by the prosecution. Then again, no resident of the place from where Rina was allegedly kidnapped by the accused persons was also examined to show if there was any such occurrence of kidnapping at about 10-00 AM at the place near the house of Kazi Sb. None of the girls who were accompanying Rina to school, were also examined. The Head Mistress of Rina's school to whom Ayah Feroja first reported the alleged kidnapping of Rina by the accused persons is also not examined to say that the Ayah reported to the Head Mistress that Rina was kidnapped by the accused persons in the manner alleged. Then again, PW 1, father of Rina, on receipt of the information 'about the alleged abduction of his daughter at first went to the school and met the Head Mistress. He then admittedly went to Thana and informed the OC (PW 3) regarding the occurrence at 11-00 AM and the DC and SP in their office and discussed the matter with them. But curiously enough, he did not lodge any First Information Report before 14-05 hours i.e. about 3 hours after the matter was reported to him and no explanation is given for this delay in lodging the First Information Report. If Rina was really forcibly abducted by the accused appellants in the manner alleged the natural conduct and logical action of the Head Mistress of the School and PW 1, the father of Rina, would be immediately to lodge First Information Report with the police for the recovery of PW 5 but neither of them did so. 

 19. The delay and the leisurely fashion in lodging the First Information Report about 3/4 hours after the occurrence along with the non-examination of the Ayah Feroja Begum and persons who are competent to prove the alleged forcible abduction, go to show that Rina was not really forcibly taken away by the accused persons in the manner alleged by the prosecution. This conclusion of ours is supported by the four letters allegedly written by Rina to accused Abdul Mannan. Rina, of course, denied to have written those letters to accused Mannan. But from a comparison and examination of the signature of PW 5 Rina in the deposition, with the original letters submitted by accused appellant Abdul Mannan at the time of his examination under section 342 CrPC we are inclined to believe the defence version that those letter were written by PW 5 Rina to accused Abdul Mannan. From the contents of the letters (some portions quoted below) it is clear that Rina was in deep and passionate love with accused Abdul Mannan to the knowledge of her parents, some relations and friends of the lovers and she was pining way for him in his absence. Admittedly, accused-appellant Abdul Mannan's residence is near the house of Rina's father. From the above evidence, facts and circumstances of the case, we are inclined to hold that the accused persons did not forcibly kidnap Rina in the manner alleged by the prosecution and Rina voluntarily went with the accused to solemnise her marriage with Abdul Mannan at Subidkhali Marriage Registrar's Office, and this is a clear case of elopement and not kidnapping and that is probably the reason as to why Rina's father took 3/4 hours time to lodge the formal First Information Report to the police station although he earlier reported the matter to PW 3 at 11-00 AM.

 Thus, under section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure no offence punishable with death, transportation or imprisonment for a term exceeding 2 years is triable summarily. In the schedules of President's Orders 8 and 50 and the Special Powers Act, 1974 grave offences like murder, rape, dacoity, etc. punishable with death and transportation for life, were also made triable summarily. In summary trials in cases where no appeal lies the Magistrates need not record the evidence of the witnesses or frame any charge as provided under section 263 and in cases in which appeal lies, the Magistrates concerned are also not required to record evidence but they are "to make a memorandum of substance of the evidence of each witness as the examination of the witness proceeds". Thus, the procedure for trying the schedule offences summarily, not only deprived the accused-persons of their fundamental and natural rights to thoroughly cross-examine the witnesses of the prosecution and recording of the evidence of each witness in the manner under section 356 of the above Code, but it also is contrary to the basic idea and principle of trial of petty cases only by the Magistrate as contemplated under section 260 CrPC. The deprivation of the accused persons to thoroughly cross-examine the witnesses of the prosecution as they are entitled under Chapter X of the Evidence Act and the failure to record the same under section 356 CrPC faithfully is likely in some cases to cause miscarriage of justice and such a method is violate of the provisions of the Evidence Act and the principles of fair trial. Because, the non-recording of evidence of witnesses as required by Chapter XXV of the Code not only greatly prejudiced the accused persons in placing their case both in the trial and appellate Court but it also prevented the prosecution to prove its case successfully and the courts from doing justice to the parties. In present case, if the learned Sessions Judge would try the accused-appellants summarily, as a Special Tribunal case as required under section 10 of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 and would not record the evidence of the witnesses under section 356 CrPC and would record only the memorandum of the substance of evidence, as required under section 355 CrPC, the accused appellants would not get the opportunity of eliciting from the prosecution witnesses by thoroughly cross-examining them that Rina was in deep love with accused Abdul Mannan and she might have also sex with him, that she was not under 16 years of age on the date of occurrence and she voluntarily eloped with accused Abdul Mannan to solemnise her marriage with him, as now appears and found from the discussion of the evidence made by us above; the accused-appellant's conviction under section 4(b) of Ordinance LX of 1983 may not be successfully assailed, as done in this Court and the poor boys, i.e. the five young appellants, would be obliged to suffer imprisonment for the rest of their life. Similar instances and chances of injustice and miscarriage of justice are not rare, in such cases, From the above, it is clear what hardship and injustice are done to such unfortunate victims charged with grave offences which are included in the schedule of the above Orders and Acts. The procedure for such summary trial of grave offences may be an emergency measure to meet certain exigencies of time, conditions and circumstances but such procedure of summary trial, cannot form part of the permanent Statute in any, civilised country having any system of law whatsoever.

 63. Chaotic condition in the legal field has been multiplied by the standard of dispensation of justice now-a-days made in the criminal courts. It may be pointed out that previously according to section 32 of the old Code, the District Magistrate or Magistrate, 1st Class had powers to inflict sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years and fine not exceeding Taka 1000.00, a Magistrate, 2nd class-imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months and fine not exceeding Taka 200.00 and the Magistrate, 3rd class imprisonment for a term of one month and fine not exceeding Taka 50.00 By change and amendment in section 32, the Magistrate, 1st Class now, may pass any sentence authorized by law except sentence of death or transportation for life and imprisonment not exceeding 10 years. It seems that the powers of the Magistrate to inflict sentence of imprisonment and fine have been inflated to keep pace with the inflation in our national economy and enemies in the country. Similarly, the Asstt Sessions Judges may now pass any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death or transportation and imprisonment not exceeding 10 years under section 31(c) and they are deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judges also under section 31(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It may be pointed out further that previously a Munsif had to serve for a period of 15-16 years to get a promotion as Subordinate Judge and he is to serve some years more after promotion for being invested with powers of trying session’s cases. But now-a-days, they are getting promotion after 7/8 years of service as Munsif. Previously, the Magistrates were to put in some years of service and to try cases as 3rd and 2nd Class Magistrates besides getting training in trial of Sessions cases and preparing certain number of case records, before they could be invested with the power of Magistrate, First Class, on the recommendation of the Sessions Judges concerned. Now-a-days due to the rapid expansion of the courts, the Munsifs are getting promotion as Subordinate Judges and Asstt. Sessions Judges after putting 7/8 years of service and Magistrates did not undergo the training and no recommendation of the Sessions Judge is now necessary for investing them with the powers of Magistrate, First Class. The Magistrate now-a days are, so to say, Magistrate's are born First Class. As a result, the standard and qualities of judgments and order passed by them in disposing of criminal cases are such that their predecessors who served in the criminal judiciary only 10 years ago, would be bound to hang their heads in shame, in seeing that the judiciary in which they once served, has come to such a low pass and standard. It may be noted that the standard of education has deteriorated to an alarming extent from the days of the former Judges and Magistrates. It has come to my notice that in petty cases in which summons are to be issued at the first instance, warrants are issued at random and accused persons are refused bail in such cases. After the abolition of procedure for trial of warrant cases as provided under Chapter XXI and the amendment made in Chapter XX amalgamating the procedure for trial of both warrant and summons cases, the provision of acquittal of accused persons under section 247 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for non-appearance of the complainant, is retained even in cases formally tried under Chapter XXI. As a result, it is found that in cases of serious offences such as assault under section 326, attempt to murder under section 307, rape, etc. which are now triable by Magistrates, First Class the accused persons are acquitted, in absence of the complainants even on off dates and in spite of filing petition for adjournments on the ground of illness, etc. Formerly, in the police cases and other serious cases, the Magistrate was obliged to procure the production of the prosecution witnesses but that is now dispensed with. As a result, criminals charged with serious offences are acquitted, without trial and thus go unpunished.

I propose to deal with the question of jurisdiction before I embark upon a discussion on merits of the case as the facts of this case has, in great detail, been narrated by my learned brother in his judgment I need not re-narrate the same to burden the judgment further. In order to express opinion on the question of jurisdiction a close examination of several provisions of the Special Powers Act, 1974, the Ordinance, the Criminal Procedure Code, 1898 and the Penal Code, 1860 is necessary. Sub-section (1) of section 26 of the Special Powers Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure or in any other law for the time being in force, the offence specified in the Schedule of the Act shall be exclusively triable by Special Tribunal constituted under sub-section (2). Sub-section (2) provides that every Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge and Assistant Sessions Judge shall, for the areas within his Sessions Division, he a Special Tribunal for the trial of offence triable under this Act. By Article 10 of the Ordinance a new paragraph No. 4B, by amendment of Special Powers Act, 1974, has been inserted in its Schedule and thereby the offence under Article 4(b) of the Ordinance which is included in paragraph No. 4,B of the Schedule has been made exclusively triable by the Special Tribunal. Article 3 of the Ordinance provides that words and expressions used in the Ordinance shall have the same meaning as in the Penal Code, 1860. The contention that by reason of sub-section (2) of section 26 of the Special Powers Act the Sessions Judge is 'ex-officio Tribunal' and as such, had jurisdiction to try the case and the trial was not vitiated for want of jurisdiction and if it had committed any error by holding such trial and by registering the case as sessions case it was a mere irregularity. This brings me to explain what is meant by jurisdiction of a court. The word 'Jurisdiction' and error within jurisdiction' are not synonymous,. The former means the very authority of the court or the tribunal to decide a matter and the latter relates to illegality committed by the court or tribunal in exercising its authority which has a valid foundation in law in deciding a case. The existence of jurisdiction is different from exercise of jurisdiction. Failure to comply with the statutory requirements in assumption of jurisdiction and in exercise of jurisdiction is visited with different legal consequences. To borrow the words of their Lordships of the Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Haridyvnath Nath Roy vs. Rani Chandra Barma Sarnia, 1921 (Cal) 34 Jurisdiction of a court and error in exercise of jurisdiction mean:   the authority to deal with the matter at all is what makes up jurisdiction. The decision of all other questions in that matter is only an exercise of that jurisdiction and in exercising of that jurisdiction if the court commits error that becomes error within jurisdiction. The authority to decide a cause at all and not the decision rendered therein is what makes up jurisdiction; and when there is jurisdiction of the person and subject matter, the decision of all other questions arising in the case is but an exercise of that jurisdiction. The extent to which the conditions essential for creating and raising the jurisdiction of a court or the restraints attaching to the mode of exercise of that jurisdiction, should be included in the conception of jurisdiction itself, is sometimes a question of great nicety". In the case of the Government of Bangladesh vs. Samir & Co. 28 DLR (AD) 21, their Lordships of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh have observed: 

 The Special Powers Act, 1974, is a special legislation whereas the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Penal Code are general legislations. The Code of Criminal Procedure, a general law and a procedural law, is an earlier Act than the Ordinance No LX of 1983 which is a special enactment and a substantive law. When an Act is passed for special reason, applying to special persons and setting up a Court or a Special Tribunal, It is not difficult to appreciate the object which the Parliament or the law making authority had in mind in placing certain matters solely within the jurisdiction of the Court or the Special Tribunal so set up preventing the other Courts from exercising jurisdiction in respect of those matters. It is a well known canon of interpretation of Statute that a special law overrides the general law.  73. By enactment of the Special Powers Act, 1974 the Parliament conferred the said jurisdiction in trying cases for offences mentioned in that Act and the Schedule thereunder upon the Special Tribunal. Therefore it seems to me, that it is the Special Tribunal and no other authority or forum has jurisdiction to try the offence under Article 4(b) in view of the provisions of Article 10 of the Ordinance. The learned Deputy Attorney-General addressed the court that by virtue of sub-section (2) of section 26 the learned Sessions Judge is the ex-officio Tribunal and had the jurisdiction to try the present offence. When a Court or Tribunal without being legally vested with the authority to try any offence specified in any enactment, whether general or special, assumes the jurisdiction over such matter, it would amount to arrogating a jurisdiction to itself transgressing the bounds of its limit. In the light of the aforesaid principle. I now pass on to consider the different provisions of the Act, the Ordinance and the Code. Sub-section (2) of section 26 of Special Powers Act, 1974 describes the authorities which may be appointed as Special Tribunal but such Tribunal automatically is not constituted with those persons or authorities enumerated therein. For establishment of a Special Tribunal a further step in making a lawful order is required. Sub-section (2) also describes several authorities viz. the Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge, and Assistant Sessions Judge to constitute Special Tribunal within the Sessions Division. Viewed from that angle as well, can it be said that in a Sessions Division the authorities mentioned therein, for such provisions, will themselves constitute Special Tribunals more than one in number in such Sessions Division? The answer is to be found in the language used in sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 26 and the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 26. According to sub-section (1) offences specified in schedule to this Act shall be triable exclusively by a Special Tribunal 'constituted under sub-section (2). Proviso to sub-section (2) also empowers the Government to 'constitute one or more Additional Special Tribunals. From a close reading of the aforesaid provisions, it seems to me, that merely because of sub-section (2) the Sessions Judge does not ipso facto become an 'Ex-Officio Special Tribunal' and the offence mentioned in the Schedule of the Act can not be registered as Sessions Case to be tried by the Sessions Judge. Nor from reading the language of sub-section (2) I find any expression as 'Ex-Officio Special Tribunal' as contended. A court of law is to interpret an Act according to the plain, unambiguous and clear meaning of a word or language, if it introduces any word not found in the section of an Act while interpreting it the court travels beyond its realm and such interpretation is against the canon of interpretation of statutes. Crawford in his 'The Construction of Statutes' has very aptly said "Where the Statutes meaning is clear and explicit, words can not be interpolated. In the first place, in such a case, they are not needed. If they should be interpolated, the statute would more than likely fail to express the legislative intent, as the thought intended to be conveyed might be altered by addition of new words. They should not be interpted even though the remedy of a statute would thereby be advanced or a more desirable or just result would occur." 

 Where the court acts without jurisdiction its 'error', 'omission' or 'irregularity' is not that of a Court of competent jurisdiction' rather such defect is that of a court which suffers from want of jurisdiction which cannot be cured under section 537 Criminal Procedure Code because the section has not made any reference to the finding, sentence and order of a court which has no jurisdiction. A decision of a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Bhola vs. Lachman, 1950 All, 475 supports the above view. Similar view has also been taken in the cases reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 690, AIR 1950 (All) 477 wherein it has been held by their Lordships that by invoking provisions of section 537 Criminal Procedure Code the defect of want of jurisdiction of a court in deciding a case cannot be cured. The aforesaid observations also supports my view that the provisions of section 537 Criminal Procedure Code cannot be taken in aid in the instant case to cure the defect of the impugned judgment of the court below which lacks in jurisdiction as the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction in respect of the offence charged. Moreover, by invoking a provision of a procedure of a procedural law a court cannot be vested with jurisdiction ousting the provision of a substantive enactment which confers jurisdiction upon a court to decide a case. So viewed, section 537 Criminal Procedure Code being provision of a procedural law has no role to play in the instant case in order to cure the defect as to jurisdiction of the Sessions Judge in holding the trial of the present case. This point can also be looked into from another angle. Even if it is assumed that the Sessions Judge is clothed with the powers of Special Tribunal even then the judgment suffers from want of jurisdiction as it has no authority in law to try a scheduled offence like that of Article 4 (b) of the Ordinance and an offence under section 366A of the Penal Code because of joinder of a scheduled offence and a non-scheduled offence. The case of Talukder Abdul Aziz vs. State, 35 DLR, 127 supports the above view of mine wherein it has been held that joinder of scheduled and non-scheduled offences was illegal and also the cognizance by the Special Tribunal of both scheduled and non-scheduled offence was without jurisdiction. In Tamij Miah vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 33 DLR 203, the same view was taken. Now let me consider the contention on section 29 of the Special Powers Act. It provides that the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code, so far only as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Special Powers Act. shall apply to the proceeding of Special Tribunals, and such Special Tribunals shall have all the powers conferred by the Code on a court of session exercising original jurisdiction. Section 29 has no manner of application where the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code are inconsistent with the provision of Special Powers Act. To put on interpretation that want of jurisdiction in taking cognizance of a scheduled offence of Special Tribunal Act by the Sessions Judge is cureable would be nothing but an absurd construction. In a clear and unambiguous language section 29 has made the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code applicable to a Special Tribunal and not to a Court of Sessions. They are different and distinct forums. In Zahirul Huq vs. Bangladesh and others, 32 DLR (AD) 33, the learned Judges of the Appellate Division have observed: 

 79. Now, I pass on merit of the appeal. The expression 'kidnap' has been defined in section 361 of the Penal Code and one of the ingredients of the offence is the minority of the person kidnapped. If she is female her age is to be under sixteen years. The word 'abduction' has been defined is section 362 of the Penal Code and ingredients of that offence are use of force or compulsion, or deceitful means to induce any person to go from any place. The word 'takes' occurring in section 361 does not imply any force and if a female who is under 16 years of age is taken away from the keeping of her lawful guardian even on her own wish, the offence of kidnapping is established. However, taking out of the keeping of the guardian is not confined to mere physical taking. It may signify some act of the accused which may be regarded as a proximate cause of going out of the keeping of a guardian or, in other words, an act but for which the minor would not have gone. Even a girl below the age of 16 years without being forcibly taken away from the keeping of her guardian if found with the accused the offence will be complete and punishable under section 363 of the Penal Code But if the age of the girl is found to be above 16 years, there will be no such offence. Therefore, I am to see what the age of the girl Rina is In FIR her age has been stated to be 13 years by her father, PW 6 Dr. Abdul Rashid also stated that the girl stated to him that she was of 13 years age. The Medical Report Ext. 4 also shows that the girl is of about 15 years of age. These are the materials on record regarding the age of the girl. But curiously enough, the father of the girl PWI, who is the most competent person to speak about the age of his daughter, did not make any statement in court about her age. Nor the prosecution put in evidence any Birth Register or a certificate from the school showing the age or the date of birth of Rina, although such register and certificate of birth of Rina, are not conclusive evidence of the age of a person but in the facts and circumstances of this case, it seems to me, those are material evidence. PW 6 has stated in his examination-in-chief that the age of the girl is about 15 years. But in his cross-examination stated "The calculation of age is subject to errors by 2-3 years" Taking into consideration the silence on the part of the father about the age of his daughter, absence of Birth Register and the statement of the Doctor who examined the victim girl, I am led to conclude that the prosecution failed to prove conclusively that the age of the victim girl was under 16 years by any evidence whatsoever. Nor from the evidence on record I find that she was induced to go from the guardianship of her father or was forced and seduced to illicit intercourse with any of the appellants or any person. Therefore, the ingredients of sections 362 and 366A of the Penal Code also are absent. As it has already been found that the girl herself went out of her own accord without being forcibly taken away by the accused and as the prosecution failed to prove by any evidence that there was unwillingness on the part of Rina to marry accused Abdul Mannan and she was compelled by the appellant to marry him against her will I do not think that the punishment contemplated under sub-article (b) of article 4 of the Ordinance can be awarded upon the accused persons. In instant case, it seems to me, from evidence, which has in great detail been stated by my learned brother, that the victim girl Rina was in passionate love with accused Mannan and as a result of which she went out of the keeping of her parents and even she was ready to be rescued by her lover accused Mannan. This conclusion of mine gets support from the love letters written by Rina to Mannan which has already been referred to in the judgment of my learned brother. Therefore, it can be held that the accused persons did not exercise any sort of compulsion on the victim girl, Rina. She went of her own accord. Prosecution also hopelessly failed to examine the Ayah, the Head-Mistress, the crews of the launch from where the girl was recovered. Non-examination of these material witnesses also casts a serious doubt about the prosecution case. There is no evidence that the accused persons have committed the offence charged.
